unit_label: Module C unit 1 (courseware unit 17): Overview of Credit Management

facts.statement: Credit drives the national economy: it gives an entrepreneur leverage to undertake a larger project than she could without credit, accelerating production; it lets a consumer spend more than she has earned, and the increased demand drives producers; adequate and cheap credit propels the economy to a higher growth trajectory. But there is a time lag between increased demand and creation of supply, and excessive credit, especially for non-productive purposes, puts inflationary pressure on the economy, so the Reserve Bank of India sometimes uses monetary tools such as Bank rate, CRR and SLR to control credit and strike a balance between growth and inflation.

Historically private moneylenders met the credit needs of individuals in India, which caused problems such as rural indebtedness and rural landlessness, aggravated by illiteracy and financial illiteracy; with the growth of banking this was tackled to a great extent. The courseware calls the nationalisation of banks in 1969 a watershed in the flow of credit: before it, credit flowed mainly to big business houses that often had an ownership or management interest in the banks; after it, the RBI ensured more credit reached neglected sectors, and the concept of Priority Sector became an integral part of the banking system.
The unwritten principles that bankers have evolved for lending, which influence loan policies, are safety of funds, purpose, profitability, liquidity, security and risk spread.

A borrower can be an individual, a sole proprietary firm, a Hindu Undivided Family, a one person company, a partnership firm, a limited liability partnership, a joint venture through a special purpose vehicle, a private or public limited company, a statutory corporation, a trust, a real estate investment trust, a co-operative society, a club or association, a local authority, an institution or a government department. The applicable laws differ: individuals by the Indian Contract Act 1872; partnership firms by the Indian Partnership Act 1932; LLPs by the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008; a Hindu Undivided Family by the Hindu Succession Act 1956; companies by the Companies Act 2013; statutory corporations by the Acts that created them; trusts and REITs by the Indian Trusts Act 1882 and public trusts and similar Acts of the states; co-operative societies by the Co-operative Societies Act 1912 or the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act 2002 or state Acts; and clubs and associations by the Societies Registration Act or the law under which they are registered.
facts.locator: Printed p. 395, section 17.4 (the courseware gives a year for the Societies Registration Act that was not checked; no item asks for it)

facts.statement: Bank credit may be fund-based or non-fund-based. In fund-based credit there is an actual transfer of money from the bank to the borrower. In non-fund-based credit there is no transfer of money, but the commitment by the bank on behalf of the client may result in future transfer of money to the beneficiary: for example a bank guarantee issued in favour of a government department on behalf of a contractor; if the beneficiary invokes it the bank must remit the amount and the client is liable to pay the bank, so non-fund-based credit can convert into fund-based credit. Other non-fund-based forms are letters of credit, co-acceptance of bills, forward contracts and derivatives. Fund-based credit can be short-term or long-term (term loan); credit can also be classified by purpose (working capital finance, fixed asset or project finance, export finance, crop loan), by type of customer (corporate, MSME, retail, agriculture, international, institutional) and by currency (rupee credit or foreign currency credit).

Each bank formulates its own loan policy and every credit proposal must be sanctioned within its framework. The policy is influenced by market conditions, competitors' policies, the bank's own SWOT analysis and RBI guidelines. It normally contains guidelines on: exposure limits for a single counterparty and groups of connected counterparties; exposure limits for sectors (real estate, capital market, steel, cement, software and so on) fixed on the bank's perception of risk, which are reduced and fresh sanctions curtailed when perception of a sector deteriorates, possibly with exit strategies; the thrust areas and low priority areas; and discretionary powers at various levels for sanctioning credit proposals and for allowing excess drawings or ad hoc limits.
facts.locator: Printed p. 396, Loan Policy of the Bank

facts.statement: Credit appraisal answers the lender's questions: is the borrower trustworthy; what will she do with the money, is the project viable and what are the risks; the amount to give; the terms of repayment and interest rate; the covenants for monitoring; whether collateral security or a personal guarantee is needed; and how to create a charge over security and which documents to take to enforce the claim in a court of law. Its complexity depends on the amount, duration and purpose, category of borrower, risks, security and RBI guidelines. The lender normally depends on some or all of: the background, credit history and market reports of the borrower; the financial track record shown by financial statements (where unavailable, as for most individuals, the net worth and repayment capacity from assets, liabilities and sources of income); a techno-economic feasibility report (for industrial projects a detailed project report prepared by a competent agency; otherwise viability judged from past record, present financial position, income and expenditure and the bank's judgment); and the securities available, their value and realisability.

Delivery relates to the legal aspects of documentation and creation of a charge over security and to the method of delivery (a loan, or cash credit for working capital limits) and the procedures for disbursal of a term loan. Control and monitoring is necessary to ensure end use of the bank's funds and their safety; efficient monitoring also helps the borrower, and any delay in acting when an activity is not going as projected reduces the chances and amount of recovery. Credit risk is a major risk and suitable policies must identify, measure and control it within acceptable limits. Even with the best policies, credit default may occur through genuine business problems or wilful default: banks first examine rectification (regularisation of the account); if that is beyond the borrower, restructuring (longer repayment period, reduced margin, pricing concessions, additional finance) so that the enterprise becomes viable again; and if restructuring is not possible or in wilful default, recovery starts. Refinance assumes importance when liquidity is tight (norms for refinance from NABARD, SIDBI and RBI for certain priority sector advances), but the risk remains with the bank and refinance does not affect the decision on a credit proposal.

RBI guidelines on end use of funds: it is the primary responsibility of banks to ensure proper end use and to monitor the flow of funds; drawals from cash credit or overdraft accounts must be strictly for the sanctioned purpose; there should be no diversion of working capital finance for acquisition of fixed assets, investments in associate companies or subsidiaries, acquisition of shares, debentures, units of mutual funds or other investments in the capital market. Illustrative systems: scrutiny of periodical progress reports and operating and financial statements; regular visits to assisted units and inspection of securities charged; periodical scrutiny of the books of accounts of the borrowers; stock audits depending on the exposure; certificates from borrowers that funds were used for approved purposes, with prompt action on incorrect certification (which may include withdrawal of facilities and legal recourse); a separate mandate to the auditors if a certificate on diversion or siphoning is desired; and examination of diversion during internal audit and inspection of branches.
facts.locator: Printed p. 398, End Use of the Funds (the courseware presents these as RBI guidance without citing a direction; not checked against the current direction)

facts.statement: The priority sector categories in the courseware, as in the 2025 Directions: agriculture; micro, small and medium enterprises; export credit; education; housing; social infrastructure; renewable energy; and others, with weaker sections (an overlapping category) also a target. RBI decides the sectors included and the minimum share of total credit that must go to them; performance is monitored through periodic returns and reviewed in forums such as the Lead Bank Scheme. Each priority sector loan must be classified in only one of the eight categories. The common guidelines include: rates of interest in accordance with RBI directions; no loan related and ad hoc service or inspection charges on priority sector loans up to Rs 50,000 (for SHG or JLG loans the limit applies per member); a record of receipt, sanction, rejection and disbursement; acknowledgement of loan applications with a Board-prescribed time limit; and ensuring that loans are granted for approved purposes with end use monitored.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 398-404, Priority Sector and Common guidelines (the amounts in this fact were read in the courseware only; the common guideline on service charges was not checked in the Directions)

facts.statement: Targets and sub-targets for priority sector lending, computed on the basis of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) or credit equivalent of off-balance sheet exposure (CEOBSE), whichever is higher, as on the corresponding date of the preceding year. For domestic commercial banks (excluding RRBs and SFBs) and foreign banks with 20 branches and above: total priority sector 40 per cent; agriculture 18 per cent (within it 14 per cent for non-corporate farmers, of which 10 per cent for small and marginal farmers); micro enterprises 7.5 per cent; advances to weaker sections 12 per cent. Foreign banks with fewer than 20 branches have a 40 per cent total (up to 32 per cent in export credit and at least 8 per cent in any other priority sector). Regional rural banks and small finance banks have a 75 per cent total, with weaker sections at 15 per cent for RRBs. Urban co-operative banks have a total of 60 per cent, micro enterprises 7.5 per cent and weaker sections 12 per cent. The 2025 Directions apply district weights to incremental priority sector credit from FY 2024-25: 125 per cent where per capita credit is lower and 90 per cent where higher.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 404-405 and RBI_PSL_2025 paragraphs 7.1, 7.2 and 8.1 (the UCB and district-weight statements are from the Directions; the figures agree with the courseware for the banks it tabulates)

facts.statement: The courseware says MSME classification now combines investment in plant and machinery or equipment with annual turnover, with no distinction between manufacturing and service units, and quotes Gazette notification S.O. 1364(E) of 21 March 2025: a micro enterprise has investment up to Rs 2.5 crore and turnover up to Rs 10 crore; a small enterprise up to Rs 25 crore and Rs 100 crore; a medium enterprise up to Rs 125 crore and Rs 500 crore. Enterprises must register on the Udyam portal and banks are guided for priority sector purposes by the classification in the Udyam Registration Certificate; retail and wholesale trade are MSMEs for the limited purpose of priority sector lending; informal micro enterprises with an Udyam Assist certificate are treated as micro enterprises.
facts.locator: Printed p. 405, Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (MSMED) Act 2006 (the notification itself was not retrieved)

facts.statement: Credit exposure norms, as the courseware states them: to avoid concentration of credit the RBI has asked banks to fix exposure limits to specific industries or sectors and has prescribed limits on exposure to a single counterparty and a group of connected counterparties. Under the Large Exposures Framework in force from 1 April 2019, aligned with the BCBS standards, a large exposure is the sum of exposure values to a counterparty or group equal to or above 10 per cent of the bank's Tier 1 capital. The exposure ceiling is 20 per cent of Tier 1 capital for a single counterparty (the Board may allow an additional 5 per cent in exceptional cases) and 25 per cent for a group of connected counterparties; for NBFCs, 20 per cent for a single NBFC and 25 per cent for a group of connected NBFCs, with no additional 5 per cent. Two or more persons are connected counterparties if one has control over the others or if they are economically interdependent; identification by economic interdependence is mandatory where exposure to one counterparty exceeds 5 per cent of Tier 1 capital. Entities connected with the sovereign are exempt from the definition of a group of connected counterparties. Infusion of capital after the balance sheet date can be counted in Tier 1 on an external auditor's certificate. For structures such as securitisation vehicles a look-through approach applies; if a bank's exposure to a structure is 0.25 per cent or less of Tier 1 capital the structure may be treated as a single counterparty, otherwise the underlying exposures are assigned to the unknown client.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 408-409, Credit Exposures Norms (the courseware's account of the 2019 framework; the current direction was not retrieved)

facts.statement: The courseware says banks must follow the RBI Interest Rate on Advances Directions (2016, updated 12 September 2023): a Board-approved comprehensive interest rate policy; all new floating rate personal or retail loans (housing, auto and so on) and floating rate loans to micro and small enterprises from 1 October 2019 and to medium enterprises from 1 April 2020 are priced with reference to an External Benchmark-based Lending Rate (EBLR); rupee loans sanctioned and credit limits renewed from 1 April 2016 continue to be priced on the Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR) unless the bank switches to EBLR; banks may offer fixed or floating rates, and interest rates on fixed rate loans of tenor below 3 years may not be less than the benchmark rate for similar tenor. Interest rates on foreign currency advances are determined with reference to a market determined external benchmark plus spread.
facts.locator: Printed p. 410, Interest Rates on Advances (the courseware cites the 2016 Directions updated in 2023; those have since been replaced by the 2025 consolidation of RBI directions, so only the benchmark idea is taught)

payload.title: Why credit matters, and where Indian credit came from
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Credit is leverage.** It lets an entrepreneur start a project bigger than her own savings allow, and a consumer buy before earning. The extra demand pushes producers to produce more, so cheap, adequate credit lifts the economy onto a higher growth path.

**The flip side:** supply takes time to catch up with demand. Too much credit, above all for **non-productive** uses, puts **inflationary pressure** on the economy. So the RBI uses monetary tools (Bank rate, CRR, SLR) to strike a balance between growth and inflation.

**Background in India** (the courseware's account):

| Period | Credit picture |
| --- | --- |
| Earlier | **Private moneylenders** met individuals' needs; rural indebtedness and landlessness followed, worsened by financial illiteracy |
| Before **1969** | Credit flowed mainly to big business houses, often connected to the banks' ownership or management |
| After the 1969 **nationalisation** | The RBI directed credit to neglected sectors; the **priority sector** concept became part of banking |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The balance between growth and inflation is the core idea: credit for production adds supply, credit for speculation or consumption alone mostly adds demand.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can excessive credit for non-productive purposes be harmful?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It raises demand without creating matching supply, adding inflationary pressure.

payload.title: The six principles of credit
payload.core_explanation_md:
Bankers have evolved six unwritten principles that shape every loan policy:

| Principle | The question it asks |
| --- | --- |
| **Safety of funds** | Will the money come back? (the depositors' money) |
| **Purpose** | What will it be used for, and is that sound and permitted? |
| **Profitability** | Does the bank earn enough on it? |
| **Liquidity** | Can the loan be repaid when needed, matching the bank's own funding? |
| **Security** | If repayment fails, what can the bank fall back on? |
| **Risk spread** | Is the portfolio spread so that one failure does not hurt? |

Safety comes first because a bank lends other people's money.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The principles pull against each other: a very safe loan earns little, and a profitable one is often riskier. Loan policy is the balance.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the six principles of credit.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Safety of funds, purpose, profitability, liquidity, security and risk spread.

payload.title: Who can borrow, and which law governs them
payload.core_explanation_md:
A borrower may be an individual, sole proprietor, HUF, one person company, partnership, LLP, joint venture through an SPV, private or public company, statutory corporation, trust, REIT, co-operative society, club or association, local authority, institution or government department. **The law that governs the borrower decides who can sign, what the borrower can pledge and how it can be sued.**

| Borrower | Governing law (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| Individual | Indian Contract Act 1872 |
| Partnership firm | Indian Partnership Act 1932 |
| LLP | Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008 |
| Hindu Undivided Family | Hindu Succession Act 1956 |
| Company | Companies Act 2013 |
| Statutory corporation | The Act that created it |
| Trust / REIT | Indian Trusts Act 1882 (and state public trusts Acts) |
| Co-operative society | Co-operative Societies Act 1912, Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act 2002, or state Acts |
| Club / association | Societies Registration Act, or the law it is registered under |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: This is why a bank checks the constitution of every borrower before documentation: a partnership firm and a company need different documents and authorities.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Act governs partnership firms, according to the courseware?

payload.title: Fund-based and non-fund-based credit
payload.core_explanation_md:
| | **Fund-based** | **Non-fund-based** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Money moves from bank to borrower? | **Yes**, actual transfer | **No**, only a commitment |
| Examples | Cash credit, overdraft, loans, term loans | **Guarantees**, letters of credit, co-acceptance of bills, forward contracts, derivatives |
| Risk | Credit risk on the money lent | **Contingent**: may turn into fund-based |

**Why a guarantee is still credit:** a bank guarantee for a contractor in favour of a government department needs no cash now. If the beneficiary **invokes** it, the bank pays and the customer must repay the bank. A non-fund-based facility therefore always carries a chance of becoming fund-based.

**Other ways to classify credit:**

- by **period**: short-term or long-term (term loan);
- by **purpose**: working capital, fixed asset or project finance, export finance, crop loan;
- by **customer**: corporate, MSME, retail, agriculture, international, institutional;
- by **currency**: rupee credit or foreign currency credit.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Banks therefore assess and limit non-fund-based exposure like any other credit exposure, and often include it in a borrower's total exposure.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can a bank guarantee turn into fund-based credit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: If the beneficiary invokes the guarantee the bank must pay, and the customer then owes the bank that amount.

payload.title: The bank's loan policy
payload.core_explanation_md:
Every credit proposal must be sanctioned **within the framework of the bank's loan policy**. The policy is shaped by market conditions, competitors' policies, the bank's own SWOT analysis and RBI guidelines.

**What a loan policy normally lays down:**

1. **Exposure limits** for a single counterparty and for groups of connected counterparties.
2. **Sector exposure limits** (real estate, capital market, steel, cement, software and so on) set on the bank's **perception of risk**. If perception of a sector worsens, the limit is cut, fresh sanctions are curtailed, and the bank may plan to **exit** some existing accounts.
3. **Thrust areas** and **low priority areas**.
4. **Discretionary powers** at each level for sanctions, and for allowing excess drawings or ad hoc limits.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The sector limits are a live tool: they move as the bank's view of each sector changes.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a bank do to its sector exposure limit when its view of that sector turns negative?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It reduces the limit, curtails fresh sanctions to that sector, and may plan exits from existing accounts.

payload.title: Credit appraisal: the questions and the evidence
payload.core_explanation_md:
Appraisal answers seven questions:

1. Is the borrower **trustworthy**?
2. What will she do with the money: is the project **viable** and what are the **risks**?
3. How **much** should be given?
4. What **repayment terms** and **interest rate**?
5. What **covenants** will allow effective monitoring?
6. Is **collateral or a personal guarantee** needed?
7. How is the **charge created**, and which **documents** will let the bank enforce its claim in court?

**Evidence used** (some or all, depending on the case):

| Evidence | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Background, credit history, market reports** | Trustworthiness |
| **Financial track record** | From financial statements; where none exist (most individuals), net worth and repayment capacity from assets, liabilities and income |
| **Techno-economic feasibility** | A detailed project report by a competent agency for industrial projects; otherwise judgement from past record, finances, income and expenditure |
| **Securities available** | Their value and **realisability** |

The effort depends on the amount, duration, purpose, borrower category, risks, security and RBI guidelines: a small crop or vehicle loan is appraised very differently from an industrial project.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Realisability matters as much as value: security that cannot be sold quickly or at a fair price protects little.

self_check.prompt_text: Where an individual has no financial statements, how does the courseware say repayment capacity is judged?
self_check.expected_takeaway: From the net worth and repayment capacity worked out from assets, liabilities and sources of income.

payload.title: After sanction: delivery, monitoring, rectification, restructuring, refinance
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Stage | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| **Delivery** | Documentation, **charge creation**, method of delivery (loan or cash credit), disbursal of a term loan |
| **Control and monitoring** | End use of funds and safety of funds; helps the borrower too; **delay in acting** on a deviation cuts recovery |
| **Credit risk management** | Policies to **identify, measure and control** credit risk within acceptable limits |
| **Rectification** | First try to **regularise** the account |
| **Restructuring** | If rectification is beyond the borrower: longer repayment, reduced margin, pricing concessions, additional finance, so the enterprise becomes **viable again** |
| **Recovery** | If restructuring is not possible (no viability, no interest or contribution from the promoter) or in **wilful default** |
| **Refinance** | Matters when liquidity is tight (NABARD, SIDBI, RBI for some priority sector advances); the **risk stays with the bank** |

Default can arise from genuine business problems or from intentional (wilful) default; the response differs.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Refinance is a funding source, not a risk transfer, so it does not change whether a proposal should be sanctioned.

self_check.prompt_text: Does refinance remove the credit risk from the lending bank?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: even if a bank gets refinance for eligible advances, the risk remains with the bank.

payload.title: End use of funds: what banks must watch
payload.core_explanation_md:
Banks must **ensure proper end use** and **monitor the flow of funds**. Drawals from cash credit or overdraft must be **strictly for the sanctioned purpose**. In particular, working capital must **not be diverted** to:

- buying **fixed assets**;
- investing in **associate companies or subsidiaries**;
- buying **shares, debentures or mutual fund units**, or other **capital market** investments.

**Tools banks use** (illustrative):

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Scrutiny of progress reports and financial statements | Spot deviations early |
| Regular visits and inspection of charged securities | Physical check |
| Scrutiny of the borrower's books | Trace the flow |
| **Stock audits** (by exposure) | Verify stock |
| **Borrower certificates** of end use | If false, prompt action: **withdraw facilities**, legal recourse |
| **Separate mandate to the borrower's auditors** | For a certificate on diversion or siphoning |
| Internal audit and branch inspection | Examine diversion |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: This is the courseware's description of the guidance; the current wording of the RBI direction was not checked.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two uses to which working capital finance must not be diverted.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: acquiring fixed assets, investing in associates or subsidiaries, buying shares or debentures, mutual fund units or other capital market investments.

payload.title: Priority sector lending: categories, rules and targets
payload.core_explanation_md:
The **RBI decides** which sectors are priority sectors and the **minimum share of credit** they must receive, monitors banks through periodic returns, and reviews them in forums such as the **Lead Bank Scheme**.

**Eight categories:** agriculture; micro, small and medium enterprises; export credit; education; housing; social infrastructure; renewable energy; others. **Weaker sections** is an overlapping category with its own target. A loan is classified in **only one** of the eight.

**Targets** (as a share of **ANBC** or **CEOBSE**, whichever is higher, on the corresponding date of the preceding year):

| Category | Domestic commercial banks (excl. RRBs, SFBs) and foreign banks with 20+ branches |
| --- | --- |
| **Total priority sector** | **40 per cent** |
| **Agriculture** | **18 per cent**: of which **14 per cent non-corporate farmers**, of which **10 per cent small and marginal farmers** |
| **Micro enterprises** | **7.5 per cent** |
| **Weaker sections** | **12 per cent** |

Other banks: foreign banks with fewer than 20 branches 40 per cent (up to 32 per cent export credit, at least 8 per cent other); RRBs and SFBs 75 per cent; urban co-operative banks 60 per cent. **District weights** apply to incremental credit: **125 per cent** where per capita credit is low and **90 per cent** where high.

**Common guidelines:** interest rates as per RBI directions; no loan-related or ad hoc service or inspection charges on priority sector loans up to Rs 50,000; records of receipt, sanction, rejection and disbursement; **acknowledgement** of applications with a Board-set time limit; approved purposes with **end use** monitored.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Eligibility limits for each category (loan amounts, farmer definitions and so on) are laid down in detail by RBI and have been amended; look them up in the current Directions rather than learning them from older text.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the total priority sector target for a domestic commercial bank, and what is the agriculture sub-target?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 40 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE (whichever is higher) in total, and 18 per cent for agriculture.

payload.title: MSME classification: investment and turnover together
payload.core_explanation_md:
The courseware says enterprises are classified by **both** tests, with no difference between manufacturing and service units. To be in a class an enterprise must meet **both** the investment limit **and** the turnover limit.

| Class | Investment in plant and machinery or equipment | Annual turnover |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Micro** | up to Rs 2.5 crore | up to Rs 10 crore |
| **Small** | up to Rs 25 crore | up to Rs 100 crore |
| **Medium** | up to Rs 125 crore | up to Rs 500 crore |

If the investment fits micro but the turnover does not, the enterprise moves up to the class whose **both** limits it meets.

**Registration:** on the **Udyam** portal; for priority sector purposes banks go by the classification in the **Udyam Registration Certificate**. Retail and wholesale trade count as MSMEs for the limited purpose of priority sector lending. Informal micro enterprises with an **Udyam Assist** certificate are treated as micro enterprises.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The thresholds are the courseware's statement of a March 2025 notification; check the current notification before relying on them.

self_check.prompt_text: An enterprise has investment of Rs 2 crore and turnover of Rs 15 crore. Which class?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Small: its investment fits micro but its turnover exceeds the micro limit of Rs 10 crore, and both limits for small are met.

payload.title: Credit exposure norms: limits as shares of Tier 1 capital
payload.core_explanation_md:
To avoid **concentration** of credit the RBI has prescribed limits on exposure to a **single counterparty** and to a **group of connected counterparties**, as a share of the bank's **Tier 1 capital** (as the courseware states the 2019 Large Exposures Framework):

| Exposure to | Ceiling |
| --- | --- |
| A single counterparty | **20 per cent** of Tier 1 (Board may allow **5 per cent more** in exceptional cases) |
| A group of connected counterparties | **25 per cent** of Tier 1 |
| A single NBFC | **20 per cent** (no extra 5 per cent) |
| A group of connected NBFCs | **25 per cent** |

**Large exposure:** the sum of exposures to a counterparty or group that is **10 per cent or more** of Tier 1 capital.

**Connected counterparties:** two or more persons are connected if one **controls** the others, or if they are **economically interdependent** (trouble for one would cause trouble for another). Checking economic interdependence is mandatory once exposure to one counterparty exceeds **5 per cent** of Tier 1. Entities connected with the **sovereign** are exempt from being treated as a group.

**Look-through:** for securitisation and similar structures, if the bank's exposure is **0.25 per cent or less** of Tier 1 the structure itself may be treated as one counterparty; otherwise the underlying exposures go to an unknown client.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware's figures are used here as its account; the current RBI direction on credit concentration was not retrieved and may have changed.

self_check.prompt_text: What share of Tier 1 capital is the ceiling for exposure to a group of connected counterparties, as the courseware states it?

payload.title: Benchmarks for pricing advances
payload.core_explanation_md:
RBI requires a **Board-approved interest rate policy**. The idea of benchmark pricing, as the courseware describes it:

| Loan type | Pricing reference |
| --- | --- |
| New floating rate personal or retail loans (housing, auto); MSE floating rate loans from 1 October 2019; medium enterprises from 1 April 2020 | **External Benchmark-based Lending Rate (EBLR)** |
| Rupee loans sanctioned and limits renewed from 1 April 2016 | **MCLR** (Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate) unless the bank switches to EBLR |
| Foreign currency advances | A **market-determined external benchmark plus spread** |

Banks may offer fixed or floating rates; the courseware adds that fixed rates for tenor below 3 years may not be less than the benchmark for similar tenor.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware cites the 2016 Directions updated in 2023; those have since been consolidated into 2025 directions, so learn the benchmark idea and look up the current rules for any specific question.

self_check.prompt_text: Which benchmark is used for new floating rate retail loans?
self_check.expected_takeaway: An external benchmark, through the EBLR.

payload.title: Priority sector targets for a bank with ANBC of Rs 5,00,000 crore
payload.core_explanation_md: A domestic commercial bank's ANBC on the corresponding date of the preceding year is Rs 5,00,000 crore and its CEOBSE is Rs 4,80,000 crore. Find the amount of each priority sector target and sub-target.

worked_steps.description: The base is whichever of ANBC and CEOBSE is higher.
Total priority sector at 40 per cent.
Within it, non-corporate farmers at 14 per cent.
Within that, small and marginal farmers at 10 per cent.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Total Rs 2,00,000 crore; agriculture Rs 90,000 crore (non-corporate farmers Rs 70,000 crore, small and marginal farmers Rs 50,000 crore); micro enterprises Rs 37,500 crore; weaker sections Rs 60,000 crore

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the 10 per cent small and marginal farmer figure not added to the 14 per cent?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is a sub-target inside the 14 per cent, which sits inside the 18 per cent for agriculture.

payload.title: Exposure ceilings for a bank with Tier 1 capital of Rs 40,000 crore
payload.core_explanation_md: A bank has Tier 1 capital of Rs 40,000 crore. Using the courseware's norms, find the ceiling for a single non-NBFC counterparty (with and without the Board's extra allowance), for a group of connected counterparties, and the level at which an exposure becomes a large exposure.

worked_steps.description: Single counterparty ceiling at 20 per cent.
With the Board's additional 5 per cent (exceptional cases).
Group of connected counterparties at 25 per cent.
Large exposure threshold at 10 per cent.
Level above which economic interdependence must be checked (5 per cent).

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Single counterparty Rs 8,000 crore (Rs 10,000 crore in exceptional cases with the Board's allowance); group Rs 10,000 crore; large exposure from Rs 4,000 crore; economic interdependence check above Rs 2,000 crore

self_check.prompt_text: For a single NBFC, would the extra 5 per cent be available?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: for NBFCs the ceiling is 20 per cent with no additional 5 per cent.

payload.stem_md: Why does the courseware say excessive credit for non-productive purposes is a concern?

options.explanation_md: Such credit raises demand, it does not lower it.

options.text_md: It reduces the number of banks
options.explanation_md: The number of banks is not affected by the type of credit.

options.text_md: It removes the need for monetary policy
options.explanation_md: Monetary policy remains necessary to manage such pressure.

options.text_md: It puts inflationary pressure on the economy because demand rises without matching supply
options.explanation_md: Excess credit for non-productive purposes raises demand without a matching rise in supply, which adds inflationary pressure.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Excess credit for non-productive purposes raises demand without a matching rise in supply, which adds inflationary pressure.

payload.stem_md: According to the courseware, what was the main effect of the nationalisation of banks in 1969 on the flow of credit?

options.text_md: Credit flowed more to previously neglected sectors, and the priority sector concept became part of the banking system
options.explanation_md: After nationalisation in 1969 credit reached neglected sectors and the priority sector concept entered banking.

options.text_md: Credit flowed only to big business houses
options.explanation_md: Credit did not flow only to big business houses after nationalisation.
Moneylenders did not become the main lenders after nationalisation.
Lending did not stop after nationalisation.

payload.correct_explanation_md: After nationalisation in 1969 credit reached neglected sectors and the priority sector concept entered banking.

payload.stem_md: Which of these is NOT one of the six principles of credit listed in the courseware?

options.explanation_md: Safety of funds is one of the six principles.
Popularity is not among the six principles of credit; the listed ones include safety, liquidity and risk spread.
Liquidity is one of the six principles.
Risk spread is one of the six principles.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Popularity is not among the six principles of credit; the listed ones include safety, liquidity and risk spread.

payload.stem_md: A bank refuses to lend a large share of its funds to a single industry, even though the returns are high. Which principle of credit is mainly at work?

options.explanation_md: Profitability would favour lending.
Purpose concerns the use of the loan.
Spreading lending across sectors avoids concentration.
Security concerns fallback.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Risk spread limits concentration in one industry.

payload.stem_md: Which Act governs a limited liability partnership as a borrower, according to the courseware?

options.explanation_md: The Indian Partnership Act 1932 governs ordinary partnership firms.
The Companies Act 2013 governs companies.
The Indian Contract Act 1872 is the general law of contracts.
An LLP is governed by the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008.

payload.correct_explanation_md: An LLP is governed by the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008.

payload.stem_md: Why does a bank check the constitution of a borrower before documentation?

options.text_md: Different kinds of borrowers are governed by different laws, which decide who can sign and bind them
options.explanation_md: Different borrower types fall under different laws, which decide who can sign and bind them.

options.text_md: All borrowers are governed by the same law
options.explanation_md: Borrowers are not all governed by the same law.
Documentation is needed for companies too.

options.text_md: The constitution decides the interest rate only
options.explanation_md: The constitution decides far more than the interest rate.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Different borrower types fall under different laws, which decide who can sign and bind them.

payload.stem_md: Which of these is a non-fund-based credit facility?

options.explanation_md: A cash credit limit involves lending funds.
A bank guarantee creates a contingent liability and involves no immediate funds, so it is non-fund based.
A term loan involves lending funds.
An overdraft involves lending funds.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A bank guarantee creates a contingent liability and involves no immediate funds, so it is non-fund based.

payload.stem_md: A bank issues a guarantee for a contractor and the beneficiary invokes it. What happens?

options.text_md: The contractor pays the beneficiary and the bank is released
options.explanation_md: The bank must remit.
Not so on invocation.

options.text_md: The bank must pay the beneficiary and the contractor is liable to pay the bank
options.explanation_md: The non-fund-based credit converts into fund-based credit.

options.text_md: The bank pays and cannot recover
options.explanation_md: The client is liable to the bank.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Invocation converts the commitment into a payment the customer must reimburse.

payload.stem_md: Classifying credit as rupee credit or foreign currency credit is a classification based on

options.explanation_md: Purpose is working capital, project, export or crop.
Period is short- or long-term.
Customer is corporate, MSME, retail and so on.
This is the currency basis.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Rupee against foreign currency credit is a currency-based classification.

payload.stem_md: Which of these does the courseware say a bank's loan policy normally contains?

options.text_md: Exposure limits for single counterparties and for sectors, and discretionary powers at various levels
options.explanation_md: A loan policy normally sets exposure limits for single counterparties and sectors and delegates discretionary powers.
Staff salaries belong to HR policy.

options.text_md: The balance sheet of each borrower
options.explanation_md: A borrower's balance sheet is part of an appraisal, not the policy.
A depositor list is not part of a loan policy.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A loan policy normally sets exposure limits for single counterparties and sectors and delegates discretionary powers.

payload.stem_md: When a bank's perception of a sector deteriorates, the courseware says it may

options.explanation_md: Increasing the limit would raise risk in a weak sector.

options.text_md: Reduce the sector exposure limit, curtail fresh sanctions and even plan to exit some existing accounts
options.explanation_md: When a sector looks weaker the bank may cut its limit, curtail fresh sanctions and plan exits from some accounts.
Ignoring the change leaves the bank exposed.
Lending only to a weak sector would concentrate risk.

payload.correct_explanation_md: When a sector looks weaker the bank may cut its limit, curtail fresh sanctions and plan exits from some accounts.

payload.stem_md: Which of these is NOT among the questions credit appraisal is meant to answer?

options.explanation_md: Trustworthiness of the borrower is a standard appraisal question.

options.text_md: What should be the repayment terms and interest rate
options.explanation_md: Repayment terms and interest rate are appraisal questions.

options.text_md: How many branches the borrower has abroad
options.explanation_md: The number of the borrower's foreign branches is not a standard appraisal question.

options.text_md: What covenants are needed for monitoring
options.explanation_md: Covenants for monitoring are an appraisal question.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The number of the borrower's foreign branches is not a standard appraisal question.

payload.stem_md: For appraising a loan to an individual who has no financial statements, a bank judges repayment capacity mainly from

options.explanation_md: An individual typically has no audited balance sheet.
A detailed project report is for projects.
Industry rankings do not measure an individual's capacity.

options.text_md: The net worth and repayment capacity from assets, liabilities and sources of income
options.explanation_md: For an individual without statements, repayment capacity is judged from net worth, assets, liabilities and income sources.

payload.correct_explanation_md: For an individual without statements, repayment capacity is judged from net worth, assets, liabilities and income sources.

payload.stem_md: The courseware says that when the rectification of a defaulted account is beyond the borrower, the bank next examines

options.text_md: Restructuring, such as a longer repayment period, reduced margin or additional finance
options.explanation_md: If rectification is beyond the borrower, the bank looks at restructuring such as longer tenor, lower margin or more finance.
Immediate recovery in every case is not the next step.
Write off is a last resort and not the next step.
Doubling the interest would worsen the borrower's position.

payload.correct_explanation_md: If rectification is beyond the borrower, the bank looks at restructuring such as longer tenor, lower margin or more finance.

payload.stem_md: Refinance from NABARD, SIDBI or RBI for eligible advances

options.text_md: Transfers all credit risk to NABARD
options.explanation_md: Risk is not transferred wholly to NABARD.

options.text_md: Does not remove the credit risk, which remains with the lending bank, and so does not affect the decision on the proposal
options.explanation_md: Refinance does not shift credit risk; it stays with the lending bank, so the decision on the proposal is unaffected.
Appraisal is still needed.
Refinance is available only for eligible advances.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Refinance does not shift credit risk; it stays with the lending bank, so the decision on the proposal is unaffected.

payload.stem_md: Which diversion of working capital finance does the courseware say should not take place?

options.text_md: Using it to pay raw material suppliers
options.explanation_md: This is a normal use.
This is a normal use.

options.text_md: Using it to acquire fixed assets
options.explanation_md: This is a diversion.
This is a normal use.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Working capital must not be diverted to fixed assets, associates, or capital market investments.

payload.stem_md: If a borrower's end-use certificate proves to be incorrect, the courseware says the bank may take prompt action, which may include

options.explanation_md: No action would condone false certification.
Raising the limit would reward the lapse.
Waiving interest would reward the lapse.

options.text_md: Withdrawal of the facilities sanctioned and legal recourse
options.explanation_md: If an end-use certificate is false, the bank may withdraw facilities and take legal recourse.

payload.correct_explanation_md: If an end-use certificate is false, the bank may withdraw facilities and take legal recourse.

payload.stem_md: How many categories of priority sector does the courseware list, and in how many may one loan be classified?

options.text_md: Eight categories; each loan in only one
options.explanation_md: The courseware lists eight priority sector categories, and a loan is classified in only one so it is not double counted.

options.text_md: Four categories; in all of them
options.explanation_md: Four is fewer than the categories listed.

options.text_md: Eight categories; in all of them
options.explanation_md: Counting a loan in all categories would double count it.
Three categories is fewer than listed.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The courseware lists eight priority sector categories, and a loan is classified in only one so it is not double counted.

payload.stem_md: What is the agriculture target for a domestic commercial bank under the 2025 Directions, as a share of ANBC or CEOBSE (whichever is higher)?

options.explanation_md: The total priority sector target.
The agriculture target.
The micro enterprises target.
The weaker sections target.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Agriculture is 18 per cent, with 14 per cent for non-corporate farmers and 10 per cent for small and marginal farmers.

payload.stem_md: The 10 per cent target for small and marginal farmers is

options.text_md: In addition to the 18 per cent
options.explanation_md: It is not additional to the 18 per cent.

options.text_md: A target for regional rural banks only
options.explanation_md: It is not limited to regional rural banks.

options.text_md: A sub-target within the 14 per cent for non-corporate farmers, which is within the 18 per cent for agriculture
options.explanation_md: The 10 per cent small and marginal farmer target sits within the 14 per cent non-corporate target, which sits within 18 per cent for agriculture.
It is not an export credit target.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The 10 per cent small and marginal farmer target sits within the 14 per cent non-corporate target, which sits within 18 per cent for agriculture.

payload.stem_md: The total priority sector target for urban co-operative banks under the 2025 Directions is

options.explanation_md: Forty per cent is below the stated target for these banks.
Seventy-five per cent is above the stated target.
7.5 per cent is far below the stated target.
Urban co-operative banks have a 60 per cent priority sector target under the 2025 Directions.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Urban co-operative banks have a 60 per cent priority sector target under the 2025 Directions.

payload.stem_md: As the courseware states the classification, an enterprise is micro when

options.text_md: Both investment is up to Rs 2.5 crore and turnover is up to Rs 10 crore
options.explanation_md: As the courseware states, an enterprise is micro when both investment and turnover limits are met.

options.text_md: Only investment is up to Rs 2.5 crore
options.explanation_md: Investment alone does not meet the dual test.

options.text_md: Only turnover is up to Rs 10 crore
options.explanation_md: Turnover alone does not meet the dual test.

options.text_md: It is registered as a trading firm
options.explanation_md: Registration as a trading firm does not define micro status.

payload.correct_explanation_md: As the courseware states, an enterprise is micro when both investment and turnover limits are met.

payload.stem_md: For priority sector purposes banks are guided by which document for the classification of an MSME?

options.explanation_md: The bank's own rating does not classify enterprise size.
Banks use the Udyam Registration Certificate to classify an MSME for the priority sector.
Audited accounts alone do not classify size.
A Board resolution does not classify size.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Banks use the Udyam Registration Certificate to classify an MSME for the priority sector.

payload.stem_md: Under the courseware's account of the Large Exposures Framework, a large exposure is one that is

options.text_md: 5 per cent or more of total assets
options.explanation_md: Five per cent of total assets is not the test.

options.text_md: 20 per cent or more of deposits
options.explanation_md: Twenty per cent of deposits is not the test.

options.text_md: 10 per cent or more of Tier 1 capital
options.explanation_md: A large exposure is 10 per cent or more of Tier 1 capital.
One per cent of Tier 1 capital is far below the threshold.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A large exposure is 10 per cent or more of Tier 1 capital.

payload.stem_md: Which statement about connected counterparties is consistent with the courseware?

options.explanation_md: Connection is not limited to relatives.
Connection is not limited to companies.

options.text_md: Connection is never mandatory to check
options.explanation_md: Checking connection is mandatory under the framework.

options.text_md: Persons are connected if one controls the others or if they are economically interdependent
options.explanation_md: Persons are connected when one controls the others or they are economically interdependent.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Persons are connected when one controls the others or they are economically interdependent.

payload.stem_md: New floating rate retail loans such as housing and auto loans are priced, according to the courseware, with reference to

options.explanation_md: New floating rate retail loans are priced with reference to an External Benchmark-based Lending Rate.
Pricing is not left to whim.

options.text_md: A fixed rate set once for ever
options.explanation_md: A rate fixed for ever is not a floating rate.
The cash reserve ratio is a reserve requirement, not a benchmark.

payload.correct_explanation_md: New floating rate retail loans are priced with reference to an External Benchmark-based Lending Rate.

payload.stem_md: A domestic commercial bank has ANBC of Rs 3,00,000 crore, higher than its CEOBSE. What is its total priority sector target, in Rs crore, at 40 per cent?
For the same bank (ANBC Rs 3,00,000 crore), what is the agriculture target at 18 per cent, in Rs crore?
For the same bank, how much of the agriculture target is the sub-target for small and marginal farmers (10 per cent of ANBC), in Rs crore?
For the same bank, what is the micro enterprises target at 7.5 per cent, in Rs crore?
A bank has Tier 1 capital of Rs 20,000 crore. Using the courseware's norm, what is the ceiling for exposure to a group of connected counterparties, in Rs crore?
For the same bank (Tier 1 capital Rs 20,000 crore), at what exposure to one counterparty does it become a large exposure (10 per cent of Tier 1), in Rs crore?
